title: Multi-day single-cell magnetic imaging of living cancer cells using Quantum Cell Monitoring
authors: Andre Pointner, Sarah Belasi, Regine Schneider-Stock, Roland Nagy
abstract: Live-cell imaging of cellular and tissue samples relies predominantly on optical modalities, such as fluorescence, confocal, and multiphoton microscopy, in which cellular information is encoded in emitted photons. Photons scatter and attenuate in biological samples, restricting depth resolution, while the excitation light required to produce them induces photodamage that perturbs the very biology under observation. Magnetic fields, by contrast, traverse biological samples without attenuation at cellular length scales, but the imaging modality that extracts the encoded information, magnetic resonance imaging, cannot resolve individual cells. Here we present Quantum Cell Monitoring (QCM), a widefield nitrogen-vacancy magnetometry platform that encodes single-cell information in stray magnetic fields rather than emitted photons and reads it out at subcellular resolution. Integrated with a specialized live-cell incubator, QCM tracks magnetically labeled living cancer for up to 72 h through their individual magnetic field signatures. It captures single-cell mitosis and morphological remodeling, as well as cell cluster formation, splitting, and migration even within dense regions where brightfield contrast collapses. By shifting the carrier of single-cell information from propagating optical photons to static magnetic stray fields, QCM decouples cell from cellular optical accessibility and auto-fluorescence, enabling sustained live-cell observation in regimes inaccessible to optical microscopy.
summary: This paper introduces Quantum Cell Monitoring (QCM), a novel platform that uses nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond to image living cells by detecting stray magnetic fields. By shifting the information carrier from damaging optical photons to static magnetic fields, QCM enables sustained, multi-day observation of cellular processes like mitosis and migration in cancer cells. This overcomes major limitations inherent to traditional optical microscopy.
main_problem: Live-cell imaging is limited by optical damage and scattering, while magnetic resonance lacks single-cell resolution.
main_result: The Quantum Cell Monitoring (QCM) platform successfully tracks magnetically labeled living cancer cells for up to 72 hours, capturing dynamic events like mitosis and migration.
method: The technique encodes single-cell information in stray magnetic fields generated by superparamagnetic nanoparticles, detected using Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond.
model_or_system: The system uses NV centers to measure local magnetic field shifts ($\Delta f$) caused by the magnetic dipole field ($\mathbf{B}_c(\mathbf{r})$) of labeled cells. This is achieved using a specialized, integrated live-cell incubator.
key_observables: Local magnetic field strength ($\mathbf{B}_c(\mathbf{r})$) and the resulting shift in the NV center's spin resonance frequency ($\Delta f$).
important_parameters: Tracking duration up to 72 hours; single-cell detection sensitivity ($\approx 0.15 \mu	ext{T}$ noise floor); SPION labeling density ($\approx 11.85 	imes 10^4$ per cell).
main_assumptions: The magnetic field signature can be accurately modeled using the magnetic dipole field formula, and the measurement can be decoupled from optical noise and photodamage.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the magnetic labeling protocol, the sample assembly on the diamond NV layer, the resulting NV center spin resonance shifts, and the integrated live-cell incubation system.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the limitations of optical imaging, introduces QCM as a solution, details the magnetic field sensing mechanism using NV centers, and presents long-term tracking results for various cell dynamics.
why_interesting: This work represents a significant engineering and experimental application of quantum sensing (NV centers) to solve a complex problem in bio-physics, demonstrating the utility of magnetic field measurements over optical ones for long-term monitoring.
